quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: In the budget meeting, the question about travel costs couldn't be answered until the finance figures came in on Thursday. The chair said, 'Let's park that and ____ once we have the numbers.'
quests.hint: The topic isn't dropped; it is postponed to a later slot.
quests.explanation: To 'circle back' is to return to a topic later, usually after getting more information. It signals postponement, not abandonment.
quests.usageContext: Very common in modern workplace speech; can sound like jargon to some listeners.
quests.idiomOrigin: Modern business English; the image is of moving in a circle to return to the same point.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a pen tracing a loop around a topic on a whiteboard and returning to it.

quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: The detail about server permissions mattered to only two people in the room, so the manager suggested they ____ and let everyone else leave.
quests.hint: The topic is moved to a smaller separate conversation.
quests.explanation: To 'take something offline' is to discuss it privately, outside the main meeting, so it doesn't slow everyone down.
options: take it to the next level
quests.usageContext: Workplace jargon; neutral, efficient tone.
quests.idiomOrigin: From computing, where 'offline' means not connected; extended to conversations in the 1990s and 2000s.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture two people stepping out of a crowded meeting to talk in the corridor.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: The venture succeeded because each partner had something to give: one supplied the contacts, another the technology and the third the funding. Everyone had to ____.
quests.hint: Each person contributes something of value.
quests.explanation: To 'bring something to the table' is to offer a skill, resource or idea that adds value to a group or negotiation.
quests.usageContext: Common in business and job interviews; positive.
quests.idiomOrigin: From negotiating tables where participants contribute proposals.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture people placing skills and tools on a conference table.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that completes the situation.
quests.question: When the director proposed cutting the training budget, the head of HR politely objected and gave three reasons why the plan would fail. She wasn't afraid to ____.
quests.hint: She resists a proposal instead of just accepting it.
quests.explanation: To 'push back' is to resist or object to a proposal or instruction, usually in a professional way.
quests.usageContext: Neutral to positive; used in business when someone respectfully challenges.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the physical image of pushing against a force.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a person planting their feet and pushing against a big incoming wall.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: Before the reform could start, the head of department knew she needed the staff to support it, so she held four workshops to win the staff's ____.
quests.hint: The employees' commitment to the idea.
quests.explanation: 'Buy-in' means agreement and commitment from the people affected by a decision.
quests.usageContext: Workplace jargon; common in change management.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the idea that people must 'buy into' a plan like buying into a business.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture employees purchasing shares in a new idea with small tokens.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: Nobody was arguing against the plan, so the manager asked a colleague to ____ to expose any weak spots.
quests.hint: He argues the opposite on purpose to test the idea.
quests.explanation: To 'play devil's advocate' is to argue against an idea deliberately, to test its strength, even if you don't disagree.
quests.usageContext: Neutral and constructive in meetings; can annoy if overused.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the Roman Catholic Church, where a 'devil's advocate' argued against canonisation of a saint.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a person wearing tiny devil horns holding up a 'But what if…?' sign.

quests.instruction: Pick the most natural idiom for this context.
quests.question: Before agreeing to the software licence, Andrea checked every clause and small note in the contract. She always made sure to ____.
quests.hint: The details hidden in the small text matter.
quests.explanation: To 'read the fine print' is to check the small details of an agreement, where important conditions are often hidden.
quests.usageContext: Neutral and practical; used for contracts, offers and terms.
quests.idiomOrigin: From documents in which important conditions are printed in small type.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a magnifying glass over the tiniest lines of a contract.

quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: On her first week in the new department, Lena listened to everyone and observed before making changes. She wanted to ____ before making any suggestions.
quests.hint: She wants to understand the situation before acting.
quests.explanation: To 'get the lay of the land' is to learn how a situation works before acting.
options: get the lay of the land
quests.usageContext: Neutral; used for new jobs, projects and places.
quests.idiomOrigin: From surveying land before building or travelling across it.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a traveller studying a map of a new territory from a hilltop.

quests.instruction: Pick the most natural idiom for this context.
quests.question: Andre didn't realise that the suggestion he made in the meeting would take over the area another manager had been working on for months. He worried he was ____.
quests.hint: He might unintentionally offend someone whose territory he enters.
quests.explanation: To 'step on someone's toes' is to offend them by interfering in their responsibilities or area.
quests.usageContext: Neutral; common when worried about overlapping roles.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the literal act of accidentally treading on someone's foot.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture two people in a narrow corridor, one wincing beneath the other's shoe.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: The talk started well, but when the speaker kept reading the slides aloud in a flat voice, the audience lost interest and the presentation ____.
quests.hint: It failed to get any reaction.
quests.explanation: To 'fall flat' is to fail to have the effect you wanted, especially when trying to entertain or persuade.
quests.usageContext: Neutral; used for jokes, speeches and events.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the image of something that fails to rise, like a cake or joke.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a soufflé collapsing in the oven.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: At the conference, the young engineer's demonstration was so impressive that the audience gave a standing ovation. She ____.
quests.hint: The audience reacts enthusiastically.
quests.explanation: To 'bring the house down' is to cause the audience to clap and cheer wildly.
quests.usageContext: Positive; used for performances and speeches.
quests.idiomOrigin: From theatre, where a great performance was said to shake the house with applause.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a theatre audience cheering so loudly that the chandelier shakes.

quests.instruction: Pick the most natural idiom for this context.
quests.question: The manager reminded the group not to get lost in the small numbers and to remember ____: what the customer actually needs.
quests.hint: The overall goal matters more than the small details.
quests.explanation: 'The big picture' is the general situation or main idea as opposed to small details.
quests.usageContext: Neutral, very common in planning and strategy.
quests.idiomOrigin: From art and photography, where a wide view shows everything.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture someone stepping back from a huge painting to view the whole scene.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: Everything went smoothly until the contractors ran out of materials and the whole project ____.
quests.hint: Progress was completely blocked.
quests.explanation: To 'hit a brick wall' is to reach a point where progress is impossible.
quests.usageContext: Informal; common in project talk.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the image of running into a wall.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a runner face-first against a big red wall.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that completes the situation.
quests.question: After the third staff resignation, unclear priorities and constant changes, the team's leader admitted that the project had ____.
quests.hint: It moved from order into chaos.
quests.explanation: To 'go off the rails' is to become out of control or chaotic.
quests.usageContext: Informal; used for projects, behaviour and events.
quests.idiomOrigin: From trains that leave the tracks and crash.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a train leaving the track and rolling across a field.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: After a key member of the team left unexpectedly, the remaining colleagues covered her tasks and made sure nothing was missed. They had to ____.
quests.hint: They took over work that wasn't being done.
quests.explanation: To 'pick up the slack' is to do the work that someone else has left undone.
quests.usageContext: Common in teams; neutral, and often used when appreciating someone's help.
quests.idiomOrigin: From ropes, where slack is the loose part that has to be pulled tight.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a colleague pulling a loose rope tight so the load doesn't drop.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: The manager kept looking over Ali's shoulder, checking every email and asking every hour for updates. Ali felt he was constantly ____.
quests.hint: He is being watched too closely.
quests.explanation: To 'breathe down someone's neck' is to watch or check them too closely.
quests.usageContext: Informal and critical; typical of micromanagement.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the image of someone standing so close you feel their breath.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a person leaning over someone's shoulder, nose almost touching.

quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: The new director made sure nobody got comfortable: she changed the meeting agenda weekly and asked unexpected questions. She liked to ____.
quests.hint: She keeps them alert and prepared.
quests.explanation: To 'keep someone on their toes' is to keep them alert and ready for anything.
quests.usageContext: Positive or neutral; used by managers and coaches.
quests.idiomOrigin: From ballet or boxing, where being on your toes means being alert.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a boxer bouncing lightly on his toes.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: While the boss was praising the team, Marco had secretly emailed the client to complain about a colleague without warning her. He'd ____.
quests.hint: He acted secretly against her.
quests.explanation: To 'go behind someone's back' is to do something secretly, especially something that would upset that person.
quests.usageContext: Critical; used when someone acts secretly against a colleague, friend or partner.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the image of acting where the person cannot see you.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a person hiding a note behind someone's back as they walk away.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: After years as her mentor, he quietly told management about her mistakes to help himself get promoted. She felt he'd ____.
quests.hint: He betrayed her trust.
quests.explanation: To 'stab someone in the back' is to betray someone who trusted you.
options: given her a piece of his mind
quests.usageContext: Strong and emotional; used for betrayal.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the image of attacking someone from behind.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a person holding a knife behind the back of a friend.

quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: When the delivery failed, the supervisor blamed the new driver in front of the client, even though she'd given him the wrong address. She'd ____.
quests.hint: She blamed him to protect herself.
quests.explanation: To 'throw someone under the bus' is to sacrifice or blame them to protect yourself.
options: given him the benefit of the doubt
quests.usageContext: Informal and critical; common in workplaces and politics.
quests.idiomOrigin: American English from the late 20th century; the image is of pushing someone into a bus's path.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a person shoving a colleague in front of an oncoming bus.

quests.instruction: Pick the most natural idiom for this context.
quests.question: The customer service team kept redirecting the caller from one department to another, and none of them answered her question. She felt she was getting ____.
quests.hint: She's passed around without help.
quests.explanation: To 'give someone the runaround' is to avoid giving a straight answer by sending them from one person to another.
quests.usageContext: Informal and critical; common in customer complaints.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the idea of making someone run around in circles.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a phone caller being sent along a spiral of doors.

quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: Customers had complained for months about slow delivery, but the company's management never responded, and the complaints ____.
quests.hint: Nobody listened or acted.
quests.explanation: To 'fall on deaf ears' is to be ignored or not listened to.
quests.usageContext: Neutral; used for warnings, requests and advice.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the image of speaking to someone who cannot hear.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a person speaking loudly to a giant ear covered with a hand.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: The crowd at the town hall meeting was hostile, skeptical and interrupted everything the mayor said. Everyone agreed that it was ____.
quests.hint: The audience is hard to impress.
quests.explanation: 'A tough crowd' is an audience that is hard to please or persuade.
quests.usageContext: Informal; often said humorously after a joke fails.
quests.idiomOrigin: From performing arts, where comedians face difficult audiences.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a comedian with a joke and a room full of folded arms.

quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: The store's refund policy was so generous that customers with clearly false complaints were still refunded. The manager hated it but repeated the old saying, '____.'
quests.hint: It's a well-known business principle, sometimes ironic.
quests.explanation: 'The customer is always right' is a business principle stating that customers' complaints should be treated seriously. It's often used ironically when customers are wrong.
options: you get what you pay for
the squeaky wheel gets the grease
quests.usageContext: Common in retail and service; sometimes sarcastic.
quests.idiomOrigin: Associated with early department store owners such as Harry Gordon Selfridge, who popularised the slogan.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a shop sign with a smiling customer and a giant tick.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: The buyer hesitated over the price, so the seller offered free delivery and a two-year warranty at the same cost. She had ____.
quests.hint: She added extras to make it more attractive.
quests.explanation: To 'sweeten the deal' is to make an offer more attractive by adding extras.
quests.usageContext: Neutral; used in sales and negotiations.
quests.idiomOrigin: From sweetening a bitter drink or food with sugar.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a cube of sugar dropped into a small cup labelled 'offer'.

quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: After nine hours of tense talks, the two sides finally reached agreement on wages and conditions. They had managed to ____.
quests.hint: They reached agreement through long, hard discussion.
quests.explanation: To 'hammer out a deal' is to reach an agreement after difficult negotiation.
quests.usageContext: Neutral and slightly dramatic; used for politics and business.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the blacksmith's craft of hammering metal into shape.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture two people beating a piece of glowing iron into a contract shape.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: The salesperson's final call convinced the reluctant client, who signed the contract before lunch. She had ____.
quests.hint: She secured final agreement.
quests.explanation: To 'clinch a deal' is to finalise an agreement, especially when it looked uncertain.
quests.usageContext: Positive; used in sales.
quests.idiomOrigin: From clinching a nail, bending its tip to fasten it firmly; used from the 1700s.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a hand hammering the final nail of a contract.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that completes the situation.
quests.question: Instead of planning anything, the operations manager spent every day solving one urgent problem after another and never got to the cause. He was always ____.
quests.hint: He reacts to emergencies rather than preventing them.
quests.explanation: To 'put out fires' is to deal with urgent problems, often the same kind again and again. It suggests reacting instead of planning.
quests.usageContext: Common in management talk; usually implies stress and poor planning.
quests.idiomOrigin: A firefighting metaphor used in business English since the 20th century.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a manager running with a small bucket from one flaming desk to the next.

quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: The payment system crashed on the busiest shopping day of the year, and every member of staff, from the CEO to the interns, was called in to help. It was ____.
quests.hint: Everyone is needed for the emergency.
quests.explanation: 'All hands on deck' is a call for everybody available to help in an urgent situation.
quests.usageContext: Neutral, energetic; used in emergencies at work and at home.
quests.idiomOrigin: From ships, where the captain calls all sailors onto the deck in a crisis.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a captain shouting as every sailor rushes on deck in a storm.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: In the same week, their main supplier went bankrupt, a cyberattack shut down the office and half the sales team caught flu. It was ____.
quests.hint: Several bad things combine into one disaster.
quests.explanation: 'A perfect storm' is a situation in which several negative factors arrive at the same time, creating a far worse result than any alone.
quests.usageContext: Used in news and business; dramatic tone.
quests.idiomOrigin: Popularised by Sebastian Junger's 1997 book about a storm formed by three weather systems.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture three dark storm fronts merging above one small ship.
